docs.title: Process CSV Data
docs.text: Parse and analyze CSV/TSV files with type annotations, header handling, and field transformations.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You have CSV or TSV files and need to parse them with proper type handling, filter rows, aggregate values, or transform the data for further analysis.

docs.title: Basic CSV Parsing
docs.text:
Parse CSV files with automatic header detection:

# Parse CSV with headers
kelora -f csv data.csv --take 5

# Parse TSV (tab-separated)
kelora -f tsv data.tsv --take 5

docs.title: CSV with Type Annotations
docs.text:
Specify field types for proper numeric handling:

# Type annotations: :int, :float, :bool
kelora -f 'csv status:int bytes:int duration:float' data.csv

# Example with typed CSV
kelora -f 'csv status:int bytes:int duration:int' examples/csv_typed.csv --take 3

Type annotations enable: - Numeric comparisons and arithmetic - Sorting by numeric values - Proper aggregations (sum, average, etc.)

docs.title: CSV without Headers
docs.text:
Process CSV files without header rows:

# No headers - use csvnh (CSV No Header)
kelora -f csvnh data.csv

# Access by index: _1, _2, _3, etc.
kelora -f csvnh data.csv --exec 'e.timestamp = e._1; e.status = e._2.to_int()'

# TSV without headers
kelora -f tsvnh data.tsv

docs.title: Filter CSV Rows
docs.text:
Filter based on field values:

# Filter by status code
kelora -f 'csv status:int bytes:int' data.csv \
  --filter 'e.status >= 400'

# Filter by multiple conditions
kelora -f 'csv status:int duration:int' data.csv \
  --filter 'e.status == 200 && e.duration > 1000'

# Filter by text patterns
kelora -f csv data.csv \
  --filter 'e.method == "POST" && e.path.contains("/api/")'

docs.title: Aggregate CSV Data
docs.text:
Calculate statistics across rows:

# Count by status code
kelora -f 'csv status:int' data.csv \
  --exec 'track_count(e.status)' \
  --metrics

# Sum bytes transferred
kelora -f 'csv bytes:int' data.csv \
  --exec 'track_sum("total_bytes", e.bytes)' \
  --metrics

# Track unique values
kelora -f csv data.csv \
  --exec 'track_unique("methods", e.method)' \
  --metrics

docs.title: Transform CSV Fields
docs.text:
Create new fields or modify existing ones:

# Calculate derived fields
kelora -f 'csv bytes:int duration:int' data.csv \
  --exec 'e.throughput = e.bytes / e.duration'

# Normalize timestamps
kelora -f csv data.csv \
  --exec 'e.hour = to_datetime(e.timestamp).hour()'

# Extract path components
kelora -f csv data.csv \
  --exec 'e.endpoint = e.path.split("/")[1]' \
  --exec 'track_count(e.endpoint)' \
  --metrics

docs.title: Convert CSV to Other Formats
docs.text:
# CSV to JSON
kelora -f csv data.csv -F json > output.json

# CSV to logfmt
kelora -f csv data.csv -F logfmt > output.log

# CSV to JSON with selected fields
kelora -f csv data.csv --keys timestamp,status,bytes -F json

docs.title: Handle Ragged/Malformed CSV
docs.text:
Process CSV files with missing or extra fields:

# Resilient mode (default) - skip bad rows
kelora -f csv data.csv --stats

# See parsing errors
kelora -f csv data.csv --verbose

# Strict mode - abort on first error
kelora -f csv data.csv --strict

docs.title: Select Specific Columns
docs.text:
Output only desired fields:

# Select specific fields
kelora -f csv data.csv --keys timestamp,method,status

# Exclude sensitive fields
kelora -f csv data.csv --exclude-keys email,ip_address

# Reorder fields in output
kelora -f csv data.csv --keys status,method,path -F csv

docs.title: Find Slow API Calls
docs.text:
kelora -f 'csv path method status:int duration:int' api_log.csv \
  --filter 'e.duration > 1000' \
  --exec 'track_count(e.path)' \
  --keys path,method,duration --metrics

docs.title: Calculate Response Time Percentiles
docs.text:
kelora -f 'csv duration:int' data.csv \
  --window 10000 --end '
    let times = window_numbers("duration");
    print("p50: " + times.percentile(50));
    print("p95: " + times.percentile(95));
    print("p99: " + times.percentile(99))
  '

docs.title: Export Error Rows
docs.text:
kelora -f 'csv status:int' data.csv \
  --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
  -F json > errors.json

docs.title: Group by Time Windows
docs.text:
kelora -f csv data.csv \
  --exec 'e.hour = to_datetime(e.timestamp).format("%Y-%m-%d %H:00")' \
  --exec 'track_count(e.hour)' \
  --metrics

docs.title: Clean and Normalize Data
docs.text:
kelora -f csv raw_data.csv \
  --exec 'e.email = e.email.to_lower().strip()' \
  --exec 'e.status = to_int_or(e.status, 0)' \
  --exec 'e.timestamp = to_datetime(e.timestamp).to_iso()' \
  -F csv > cleaned.csv

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Type Handling: - Use :int for status codes, counts, IDs - Use :float for durations, measurements, rates - Use :bool for flags (accepts: true/false, 1/0, yes/no) - Untyped fields remain as strings

Performance: - Add --parallel for large CSV files - Use --batch-size to control memory usage - Filter early to reduce processing overhead

Error Handling: - Use --verbose to see parsing errors - Use --stats to see skip/error counts - Ragged CSV (missing fields) creates partial events

Field Access: - Headers become field names (spaces → underscores) - Without headers, use _1, _2, _3 etc. - Use to_int_or() / to_float_or() for safe type conversion

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: Complete command-line interface reference for Kelora. For quick start examples, see the Quickstart Guide.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: kelora [OPTIONS] [FILES]...

docs.title: Processing Modes
docs.text:
Kelora supports two processing modes:

Mode When to Use Characteristics Sequential (default) Streaming, interactive, ordered output Events processed one at a time in order Parallel (--parallel) High-throughput batch processing Events processed in parallel batches across cores

docs.title: Common Examples
docs.text:
# Find errors in access logs
> kelora access.log --levels error,critical

# Transform JSON logs with Rhai
> kelora -j app.json --exec 'e.duration_ms = e.end_time - e.start_time'

# Extract specific fields from NGINX logs
> kelora nginx.log -f combined --keys method,status,path

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
[FILES]...

Input files to process. If omitted, reads from stdin. Use - to explicitly specify stdin.

Examples: 

> kelora app.log                    # Single file
> kelora logs/*.jsonl               # Multiple files with glob
> kelora file1.log file2.log        # Multiple files explicit
> tail -f app.log | kelora -j       # From stdin
> kelora -                          # Explicitly read stdin

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Complete reference for Kelora's exit codes and their meanings.

docs.title: Standard Exit Codes
docs.text:
Kelora uses standard Unix exit codes to indicate success or failure:

Code Name Meaning Cause 0 Success No errors occurred Clean processing, no parse/filter/exec errors 1 General Error Processing errors occurred Parse errors, filter errors, exec errors 2 Usage Error Invalid command-line usage Invalid flags, missing files, configuration errors

docs.title: Signal Exit Codes
docs.text:
When Kelora is interrupted by signals:

Code Signal Meaning 130 SIGINT Interrupted by Ctrl+C 141 SIGPIPE Broken pipe (normal in Unix pipelines) 143 SIGTERM Terminated by system or user

docs.title: When It Occurs
docs.text:
Exit code 0 indicates successful processing with no errors:

  • All lines parsed successfully
  • No filter errors
  • No exec/transform errors
  • Processing completed normally

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log --levels info
> echo $?
0

Note: Filtering events is not considered an error. If all events are filtered out, exit code is still 0 (as long as no errors occurred).

docs.title: Filtering vs Errors
docs.text:
# This returns 0 (filtering is not an error)
> kelora -j app.log --levels critical
> echo $?
0

# This returns 1 (parse error occurred)
> kelora -j malformed.log
> echo $?
1

docs.title: When It Occurs
docs.text:
Exit code 1 indicates processing errors occurred:

  • Parse errors: Lines that couldn't be parsed in specified format
  • Filter errors: --filter expressions that failed during evaluation
  • Exec errors: --exec scripts that failed during execution

docs.title: Resilient Mode (Default)
docs.text:
In resilient mode, errors are recorded but processing continues. Exit code 1 is returned at the end if any errors occurred:

> kelora -j app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()'
# ... processing continues despite errors ...
> echo $?
1  # Errors occurred but processing completed

docs.title: Strict Mode
docs.text:
In strict mode (--strict), processing aborts immediately on first error:

> kelora -j --strict app.log
# ... aborts on first error ...
> echo $?
1  # Processing aborted due to error

docs.title: Parse Errors
docs.text:
Example: 

> echo '{"valid": "json"}' > test.log
> echo '{invalid json}' >> test.log
> kelora -j test.log
> echo $?
1  # Parse error occurred

docs.title: Filter Errors
docs.text:
Example: 

> kelora -j app.log --filter 'e.timestamp.to_unix() > 1000000'
# If e.timestamp is missing or invalid
> echo $?
1  # Filter error occurred

docs.title: Exec Errors
docs.text:
Example: 

> kelora -j app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()'
# If e.value is not a valid integer
> echo $?
1  # Exec error occurred

docs.title: When It Occurs
docs.text:
Exit code 2 indicates command-line usage errors:

  • Invalid flags: Unknown or malformed options
  • Missing required arguments: Required values not provided
  • File not found: Input files don't exist
  • Configuration errors: Invalid configuration file
  • Permission denied: Can't read input files

docs.title: Invalid Flags
docs.text:
> kelora --invalid-flag app.log
kelora: error: unrecognized option '--invalid-flag'
> echo $?
2

docs.title: File Not Found
docs.text:
> kelora -j nonexistent.log
kelora: error: failed to open file 'nonexistent.log': No such file or directory
> echo $?
2

docs.title: Invalid Configuration
docs.text:
> kelora --config-file invalid.ini app.log
kelora: error: failed to parse configuration file
> echo $?
2

docs.title: Exit Code 130: SIGINT (Ctrl+C)
docs.text:
User interrupted processing with Ctrl+C:

> kelora -j large.log
# Press Ctrl+C
^C
> echo $?
130

docs.title: Exit Code 141: SIGPIPE (Broken Pipe)
docs.text:
Output pipe closed (normal in Unix pipelines):

> kelora -j large.log | head -n 10
# Kelora receives SIGPIPE when head closes
> echo $?
141

Note: Exit code 141 is normal in pipelines and typically not an error condition.

docs.title: Exit Code 143: SIGTERM
docs.text:
Process terminated by system or user:

> kelora -j large.log &
[1] 12345
> kill 12345
[1]+  Terminated              kelora -j large.log
> echo $?
143

    *)
        echo "✗ Unknown error (exit code: $exit_code)"
        exit $exit_code

esac

# Check for errors in logs

kelora -qq -j app.log --levels error,critical
exit_code=$?

if [ $exit_code -eq 1 ]; then
    echo "✗ Parse errors in log file"
    exit 1

fi

echo "✓ No critical issues"

docs.title: Automation with Retry

#!/bin/bash
# Process logs with retry on failure

max_attempts=3
attempt=1

while [ $attempt -le $max_attempts ]; do
    if kelora -j app.log -F json > output.json; then
        echo "✓ Processing succeeded"
        exit 0
    else
        echo "✗ Attempt $attempt failed"
        attempt=$((attempt + 1))
        sleep 5
    fi
done

echo "✗ Processing failed after $max_attempts attempts"
exit 1

docs.title: Conditional Processing
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# Process only if no errors

if kelora -qq -j --strict app.log; then
    echo "✓ No errors, processing..."
    kelora -j app.log --exec 'track_count(e.service)' --metrics
else
    echo "✗ Errors detected, skipping processing"
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Exit Code 1 When Expecting 0
docs.text:
Problem: Getting exit code 1 but don't see errors.

Solution: Use --verbose to see errors: 

> kelora -j --verbose app.log

Or check stats: 

> kelora -j --stats app.log

docs.title: Exit Code 141 in Pipelines
docs.text:
Problem: Getting exit code 141 (SIGPIPE) in pipelines.

This is normal: When downstream commands close the pipe (like head), Kelora receives SIGPIPE.

> kelora -j large.log | head -n 10
# Exit code 141 is normal here

To ignore SIGPIPE: 

> kelora -j large.log | head -n 10 || [ $? -eq 141 ]

docs.title: Exit Code 2 with Valid Syntax
docs.text:
Problem: Getting exit code 2 but command looks correct.

Check: - File exists and is readable - Configuration file is valid - Permissions are correct

> ls -l app.log
> kelora -j app.log

docs.title: Different Exit Codes in CI vs Local
docs.text:
Problem: Different exit codes in CI/CD vs local development.

Possible causes: - Different file permissions - Different file paths - Different configuration files - Different environment variables

Solution: Test with same conditions: 

> kelora --ignore-config -j app.log  # Ignore config files

docs.title: Format Reference
docs.text: Complete reference for all input formats supported by Kelora.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Kelora supports multiple input formats for parsing log files:

Format Description Use Case json JSON lines (one object per line) Application logs, structured data line Plain text (default) Unstructured logs, raw text logfmt Key-value pairs Heroku-style logs, simple structured logs csv / tsv Comma/tab-separated values Spreadsheet data, exports syslog Syslog RFC5424 and RFC3164 System logs, network devices combined Apache/Nginx combined format Web server access logs clf Apache Common Log Format Web server access logs cef ArcSight Common Event Format Security logs, SIEM data cols:<spec> Custom column parsing Fixed-width or delimited logs auto Auto-detect format Mixed or unknown formats

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
-f json
# or shorthand:
-j

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse each line as a JSON object. Nested structures are preserved.

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
{"timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z", "level": "ERROR", "service": "api", "message": "Connection failed"}
{"timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:01Z", "level": "INFO", "service": "db", "message": "Query executed"}

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: All JSON fields become event fields with their original names and types.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log --levels error
> kelora -f json app.log --keys timestamp,level,message

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• One JSON object per line (JSON Lines format)
  • Supports nested objects and arrays
  • Preserves field types (strings, numbers, booleans, null)
  • Use with -M json for multi-line JSON objects

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
-f line
# (default if no format specified)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse each line as plain text. Each line becomes an event with a single line field.

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
2024-01-15 10:30:00 ERROR Connection failed
2024-01-15 10:30:01 INFO Query executed

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: • line - The complete line as a string

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora app.log --filter 'e.line.contains("ERROR")'
> kelora -f line app.log --exec 'e.level = e.line.extract_re(r"(ERROR|INFO|WARN)")'

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Default format when no -f is specified
  • Empty lines are skipped
  • Useful for unstructured logs or custom parsing

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f logfmt

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse Heroku-style key-value pairs (logfmt format).

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
timestamp=2024-01-15T10:30:00Z level=ERROR service=api message="Connection failed"
timestamp=2024-01-15T10:30:01Z level=INFO service=db message="Query executed"

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: All key-value pairs become top-level fields.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -f logfmt app.log --levels error
> kelora -f logfmt app.log --keys timestamp,service,message

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Supports quoted values with spaces: key="value with spaces"
  • Unquoted values end at whitespace
  • Keys must be alphanumeric (with underscores/hyphens)

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
-f csv        # Comma-separated with header
-f tsv        # Tab-separated with header
-f csvnh      # CSV without header
-f tsvnh      # TSV without header

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse comma-separated or tab-separated values. First line is used as header (unless nh variant).

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
With header: 

timestamp,level,service,message
2024-01-15T10:30:00Z,ERROR,api,Connection failed
2024-01-15T10:30:01Z,INFO,db,Query executed

Without header: 

2024-01-15T10:30:00Z,ERROR,api,Connection failed
2024-01-15T10:30:01Z,INFO,db,Query executed

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: With header: Field names from header row Without header: col_0, col_1, col_2, etc.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -f csv data.csv --levels error
> kelora -f csvnh data.csv --keys col_0,col_1,col_2

docs.title: Type Annotations
docs.text:
Specify field types for automatic conversion:

> kelora -f 'csv status:int bytes:int response_time:float' access.csv

Supported types: - int - Parse as integer - float - Parse as floating-point number - bool - Parse as boolean

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Quoted fields supported: "value, with, commas"
  • Escaped quotes: "value with ""quotes"""
  • Empty fields become empty strings

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f syslog

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse syslog messages (RFC5424 and RFC3164).

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
RFC5424: 

<165>1 2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z myhost myapp 1234 ID47 - Connection failed

RFC3164: 

<34>Jan 15 10:30:00 myhost myapp[1234]: Connection failed

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text:
RFC5424: - facility - Syslog facility code - severity - Syslog severity level - timestamp - Parsed timestamp - hostname - Source hostname - appname - Application name - procid - Process ID - msgid - Message ID - message - Log message

RFC3164: - facility - Syslog facility code - severity - Syslog severity level - timestamp - Parsed timestamp - hostname - Source hostname - tag - Syslog tag (usually appname[pid]) - message - Log message

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -f syslog /var/log/syslog --filter 'e.severity <= 3'
> kelora -f syslog messages.log --keys timestamp,hostname,appname,message

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Auto-detects RFC5424 vs RFC3164
  • Severity levels: 0=emerg, 1=alert, 2=crit, 3=err, 4=warn, 5=notice, 6=info, 7=debug

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f combined

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse Apache/Nginx combined log format (web server access logs).

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
Apache Combined: 

192.168.1.1 - user [15/Jan/2024:10:30:00 +0000] "GET /api/data HTTP/1.1" 200 1234 "http://example.com/" "Mozilla/5.0"

Nginx with request_time: 

192.168.1.1 - - [15/Jan/2024:10:30:00 +0000] "GET /api/data HTTP/1.1" 200 1234 "-" "curl/7.68.0" "0.123"

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text:
• ip - Client IP address
  • identity - RFC 1413 identity (usually -)
  • user - HTTP authenticated username (or -)
  • timestamp - Request timestamp
  • request - Full HTTP request line
  • method - HTTP method (extracted from request)
  • path - Request path (extracted from request)
  • protocol - HTTP protocol version (extracted from request)
  • status - HTTP status code
  • bytes - Response size in bytes (or -)
  • referer - HTTP referer header (or -)
  • user_agent - HTTP user agent header
  • request_time - Request processing time in seconds (Nginx only, or -)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log --filter 'e.status >= 400'
> kelora -f combined access.log --keys ip,status,request,request_time

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Supports Apache Common Log Format (subset of combined)
  • Auto-extracts method, path, protocol from request line
  • request_time only available in Nginx logs with custom format

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f clf

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse Apache Common Log Format (older format without referer/user-agent).

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: Same as combined format, but without referer, user_agent, request_time.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: > kelora -f clf /var/log/apache2/access.log --filter 'e.status == 404'

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f cef

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse ArcSight Common Event Format (security logs).

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text: CEF:0|Security|threatmanager|1.0|100|worm successfully stopped|10|src=10.0.0.1 dst=2.1.2.2 spt=1232

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text:
• cef_version - CEF format version
  • device_vendor - Device vendor name
  • device_product - Device product name
  • device_version - Device version
  • signature_id - Event signature ID
  • name - Event name
  • severity - Event severity
  • Plus all extension fields as top-level fields

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
> kelora -f cef security.log --filter 'e.severity > 5'
> kelora -f cef security.log --keys timestamp,name,src,dst

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f 'cols:<spec>'

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Parse custom column-based formats with field specifications.

docs.title: Specification Syntax
docs.text:
cols:field1:width field2:width field3:*

Width types: - N - Fixed width of N characters - :ts - Timestamp field (special handling) - * - Remainder of line (greedy)

docs.title: Input Example
docs.text:
Fixed-width: 

2024-01-15T10:30:00Z ERROR Connection failed

Spec: 

-f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 message:*'

Whitespace-delimited: 

ERROR api "Connection failed"

Spec: 

-f 'cols:level service message'

docs.title: Output Fields
docs.text: Field names from specification.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Fixed-width columns
> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 message:*' app.log

# Whitespace-delimited
> kelora -f 'cols:level service message' app.log

# Custom separator
> kelora -f 'cols:name age city' --cols-sep ',' data.txt

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Default separator: whitespace
  • Use --cols-sep to specify custom separator
  • :ts extracts timestamp field automatically
  • * must be last field (consumes remainder)

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: -f auto

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Automatically detect input format from first line.

docs.title: Detection Order
docs.text:
1. JSON (if line starts with {)
  2. Syslog (if line starts with <NNN>)
  3. CEF (if line starts with CEF:)
  4. Combined/CLF (if matches Apache/Nginx pattern)
  5. Logfmt (if contains key=value pairs)
  6. CSV (if contains commas with consistent pattern)
  7. Line (fallback)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: > kelora -f auto mixed.log --levels error

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Detects format from first non-empty line
  • Uses same format for all subsequent lines
  • Not suitable for files with mixed formats

docs.title: --ts-field <field>
docs.text:
Specify custom timestamp field name:

> kelora -j --ts-field created_at app.log

docs.title: --ts-format <format>
docs.text:
Specify custom timestamp format (chrono format strings):

> kelora --ts-format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' app.log
> kelora --ts-format '%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z' access.log

See --help-time for format reference.

docs.title: --input-tz <timezone>
docs.text:
Timezone for naive timestamps:

> kelora --input-tz local app.log
> kelora --input-tz Europe/Berlin app.log

docs.title: --cols-sep <separator>
docs.text:
Column separator for cols:<spec> format:

> kelora -f 'cols:name age city' --cols-sep '|' data.txt

docs.title: --extract-prefix <field>
docs.text:
Extract text before separator into field (before parsing):

> docker compose logs | kelora --extract-prefix service -j

docs.title: --prefix-sep <separator>
docs.text:
Prefix separator (default: |):

> kelora --extract-prefix node --prefix-sep ' :: ' cluster.log

docs.title: -M, --multiline <strategy>
docs.text:
Multi-line event detection:

> kelora -M json app.log              # Multi-line JSON objects
> kelora -M '^\\d{4}-' app.log        # Events start with year
> kelora -M '^\\S' app.log            # Events start with non-whitespace

See --help-multiline for strategy reference.

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text: Control how Kelora outputs events:

docs.title: -F, --output-format <format>
docs.text: Format Description default Key-value format with colors (default) json JSON lines (one object per line) logfmt Key-value pairs (logfmt format) inspect Debug format with type information levelmap Grouped by log level csv CSV with header tsv Tab-separated values with header csvnh CSV without header tsvnh TSV without header none No output (useful with --stats or --metrics)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Output as JSON
> kelora -j app.log -F json

# Output as CSV
> kelora -j app.log -F csv --keys timestamp,level,message

# No event output, only stats
> kelora -j app.log -F none --stats

docs.title: Format Conversion
docs.text:
Convert between formats by combining input and output formats:

# JSON to CSV
> kelora -j app.log -F csv --keys timestamp,level,message > output.csv

# Logfmt to JSON
> kelora -f logfmt app.log -F json > output.jsonl

# CSV to Logfmt
> kelora -f csv data.csv -F logfmt > output.log

# Combined log to JSON
> kelora -f combined access.log -F json > access.jsonl

docs.title: Parse JSON with Auto-Detection
docs.text: > kelora -f auto app.log --levels error

docs.title: Parse Web Logs and Filter
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400' \
    --keys ip,status,request

docs.title: Parse CSV with Type Conversion
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'csv status:int bytes:int' data.csv \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400'

docs.title: Parse Custom Format
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 service:10 message:*' app.log \
    --levels error

docs.title: Parse Syslog and Extract
docs.text:
> kelora -f syslog /var/log/syslog \
    --filter 'e.severity <= 3' \
    --keys timestamp,hostname,message

docs.title: Parse with Prefix Extraction
docs.text:
> docker compose logs | kelora --extract-prefix container -j \
    --filter 'e.container == "web_1"'

docs.title: Format Not Detected
docs.text:
Problem: Auto-detection picks wrong format.

Solution: Specify format explicitly: 

> kelora -f json app.log

docs.title: Timestamp Not Parsed
docs.text:
Problem: Timestamps not recognized.

Solution: Specify timestamp format: 

> kelora --ts-format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' app.log

docs.title: CSV Parsing Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Quoted fields not handled correctly.

Solution: Ensure CSV is properly formatted with standard quoting: 

"field with, comma","another field"

docs.title: Multi-line Events
docs.text:
Problem: Single event spans multiple lines.

Solution: Use multi-line mode: 

> kelora -M json app.log

docs.title: Mixed Formats
docs.text:
Problem: Log file contains multiple formats.

Solution: Use preprocessing or separate files: 

> grep '^{' mixed.log | kelora -j --levels error
> grep -v '^{' mixed.log | kelora -f line

docs.title: text.extract_re(pattern [, group])
docs.text:
Extract first regex match or capture group.

e.error_code = e.message.extract_re(r"ERR-(\d+)", 1)  // "ERR-404" → "404"
e.full_match = e.line.extract_re(r"\d{3}")            // First 3-digit number

docs.title: text.extract_all_re(pattern [, group])
docs.text:
Extract all regex matches as array.

e.numbers = e.line.extract_all_re(r"\d+")             // All numbers
e.codes = e.message.extract_all_re(r"ERR-(\d+)", 1)   // All error codes

docs.title: text.extract_re_maps(pattern, field)
docs.text:
Extract regex matches as array of maps for fan-out with emit_each().

// Extract all error codes with context
let errors = e.log.extract_re_maps(r"(?P<code>ERR-\d+): (?P<msg>[^\n]+)", "error");
emit_each(errors)  // Each match becomes an event with 'code' and 'msg' fields

docs.title: text.extract_ip([nth])
docs.text:
Extract IP address from text (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.client_ip = e.headers.extract_ip()                  // First IP
e.origin_ip = e.forwarded.extract_ip(-1)              // Last IP

docs.title: text.extract_ips()
docs.text:
Extract all IP addresses as array.

e.all_ips = e.headers.extract_ips()                   // ["192.168.1.1", "10.0.0.1"]

docs.title: text.extract_url([nth])
docs.text:
Extract URL from text (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.link = e.message.extract_url()                      // First URL

docs.title: text.extract_domain()
docs.text:
Extract domain from URL or email address.

e.domain = "https://api.example.com/path".extract_domain()  // "example.com"
e.mail_domain = "user@corp.example.com".extract_domain()    // "corp.example.com"

docs.title: text.before(delimiter [, nth])
docs.text:
Text before occurrence of delimiter (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.user = e.email.before("@")                          // "user@host.com" → "user"
e.path = e.url.before("?")                            // Strip query string

docs.title: text.after(delimiter [, nth])
docs.text:
Text after occurrence of delimiter (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.extension = e.filename.after(".")                   // "file.txt" → "txt"
e.domain = e.email.after("@")                         // "user@host.com" → "host.com"

docs.title: text.between(start, end)
docs.text:
Text between start and end delimiters.

e.quoted = e.line.between('"', '"')                   // Extract quoted string

docs.title: text.starting_with(prefix [, nth])
docs.text:
Return substring from prefix to end (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.from_error = e.log.starting_with("ERROR:")          // "INFO: ok ERROR: bad" → "ERROR: bad"

docs.title: text.ending_with(suffix [, nth])
docs.text:
Return substring from start to end of suffix (nth: 1=first, -1=last).

e.up_to_end = e.log.ending_with(".txt")               // "file.txt more" → "file.txt"

docs.title: text.slice(spec)
docs.text:
Slice text using Python notation (e.g., "1:5", ":3", "-2:").

e.first_three = e.code.slice(":3")                    // "ABCDEF" → "ABC"
e.last_two = e.code.slice("-2:")                      // "ABCDEF" → "EF"
e.middle = e.code.slice("2:5")                        // "ABCDEF" → "CDE"

docs.title: text.col(spec [, separator])
docs.text:
Extract columns by index/range/list (e.g., '1', '1,3,5', '1:4').

e.first = e.line.col("1")                             // First column (1-indexed)
e.cols = e.line.col("1,3,5")                          // Columns 1, 3, 5
e.range = e.line.col("2:5", "\t")                     // Columns 2-5, tab-separated

docs.title: text.parse_json()
docs.text:
Parse JSON string into map/array.

e.data = e.payload.parse_json()
e.value = e.data["key"]

docs.title: text.parse_logfmt()
docs.text:
Parse logfmt line into structured fields.

let fields = e.line.parse_logfmt()
e.level = fields["level"]

docs.title: text.parse_syslog()
docs.text:
Parse syslog line into structured fields.

let syslog = e.line.parse_syslog()
e.priority = syslog["priority"]
e.message = syslog["message"]

docs.title: text.parse_combined()
docs.text:
Parse Apache/Nginx combined log line.

let access = e.line.parse_combined()
e.ip = access["ip"]
e.status = access["status"]

docs.title: text.parse_cef()
docs.text:
Parse Common Event Format line into fields.

let cef = e.line.parse_cef()
e.severity = cef["severity"]

docs.title: text.parse_kv([sep [, kv_sep]])
docs.text:
Parse key-value pairs from text.

e.params = e.query.parse_kv("&", "=")                 // "a=1&b=2" → {a: "1", b: "2"}

docs.title: text.parse_url()
docs.text:
Parse URL into structured components.

let url = e.request.parse_url()
e.scheme = url["scheme"]
e.host = url["host"]
e.path = url["path"]

docs.title: text.parse_query_params()
docs.text:
Parse URL query string into map.

e.params = e.query_string.parse_query_params()        // "a=1&b=2" → {a: "1", b: "2"}

docs.title: text.parse_email()
docs.text:
Parse email address into parts.

let email = "User Name <user@example.com>".parse_email()
e.name = email["name"]       // "User Name"
e.address = email["address"] // "user@example.com"

docs.title: text.parse_user_agent()
docs.text:
Parse common user-agent strings into components.

let ua = e.user_agent.parse_user_agent()
e.browser = ua["browser"]
e.os = ua["os"]

docs.title: text.parse_jwt()
docs.text:
Parse JWT header/payload without verification.

let jwt = e.token.parse_jwt()
e.user_id = jwt["payload"]["sub"]

docs.title: text.parse_path()
docs.text:
Parse filesystem path into components.

let path = "/var/log/app.log".parse_path()
e.dir = path["dir"]          // "/var/log"
e.file = path["file"]        // "app.log"

docs.title: text.parse_media_type()
docs.text:
Parse media type tokens and parameters.

let mt = "text/html; charset=utf-8".parse_media_type()
e.type = mt["type"]          // "text"
e.subtype = mt["subtype"]    // "html"

docs.title: text.parse_content_disposition()
docs.text:
Parse Content-Disposition header parameters.

let cd = e.header.parse_content_disposition()
e.filename = cd["filename"]

docs.title: text.encode_b64() / text.decode_b64()
docs.text:
Base64 encoding/decoding.

e.encoded = e.data.encode_b64()
e.decoded = e.payload.decode_b64()

docs.title: text.encode_hex() / text.decode_hex()
docs.text:
Hexadecimal encoding/decoding.

e.hex = e.bytes.encode_hex()
e.bytes = e.hex_string.decode_hex()

docs.title: text.encode_url() / text.decode_url()
docs.text:
URL percent encoding/decoding.

e.encoded = e.param.encode_url()                      // "hello world" → "hello%20world"
e.decoded = e.url_param.decode_url()

docs.title: text.escape_json() / text.unescape_json()
docs.text:
JSON escape sequence handling.

e.escaped = e.text.escape_json()
e.unescaped = e.json_string.unescape_json()

docs.title: text.escape_html() / text.unescape_html()
docs.text:
HTML entity escaping/unescaping.

e.safe = e.user_input.escape_html()                   // "<script>" → "<script>"
e.text = e.html_entity.unescape_html()

docs.title: text.hash([algo])
docs.text:
Hash with algorithm (default: sha256, also: sha1, md5, xxh3, blake3).

e.checksum = e.content.hash()                         // SHA-256
e.md5 = e.file.hash("md5")
e.fast = e.data.hash("xxh3")                          // Fast non-crypto hash

docs.title: text.bucket()

docs.text: Quick reference for Rhai scripting in Kelora. For detailed tutorials, see Scripting Transforms. For practical examples: kelora --help-examples. For function reference: kelora --help-functions.

docs.title: Variables & Types
docs.text:
let x = 42;                          // Integer (i64)
let price = 19.99;                   // Float (f64)
let name = "alice";                  // String (double quotes only!)
let active = true;                   // Boolean (true/false)
let tags = [1, "two", 3.0];          // Array (mixed types ok)
let user = #{name: "bob", age: 30};  // Map/object literal
let empty = ();                      // Unit type (Rhai's "nothing")

type_of(x)                           // Returns: "i64", "string", "array", "map", "()"
x = "hello";                         // Dynamic typing: can change type

Key Points:

  • let required for new variables (no implicit declaration)
  • Double quotes only for strings ("text" not 'text')
  • Unit type () represents "nothing" (not null/undefined)
  • Arrays and maps are reference types (modifying copies affects original)

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
// Arithmetic
a + b    a - b    a * b    a / b    a % b    a ** b  // power: 2**3 == 8

// Comparison
a == b   a != b   a < b    a > b    a <= b   a >= b

// Logical
a && b   a || b   !a

// Bitwise
a & b    a | b    a ^ b    a << b   a >> b

// Assignment
a = b    a += b   a -= b   a *= b   a /= b   a %= b
a &= b   a |= b   a ^= b   a <<= b  a >>= b

// Ranges (for loops only)
1..5     // Exclusive: 1, 2, 3, 4
1..=5    // Inclusive: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

// Membership
"key" in map                         // Check if key exists

docs.title: If-Else
docs.text:
if x > 10 {
    print("big");
} else if x > 5 {
    print("medium");
} else {
    print("small");
}

// Ternary-style (if is an expression)
let category = if x > 10 { "big" } else { "small" };

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
let category = switch x {
    1 => "one",
    2 | 3 => "two or three",          // Multiple cases
    4..=6 => "four to six",            // Range matching
    _ => "other"                       // Default (underscore)
};

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
// Range loops
for i in 0..10 { print(i); }          // 0 to 9
for i in 0..=10 { print(i); }         // 0 to 10

// Array iteration
for item in array { print(item); }

// Map iteration
for (key, value) in map {
    print(`${key} = ${value}`);
}

// While loop
while condition {
    if done { break; }
    if skip { continue; }
}

// Infinite loop
loop {
    if should_stop { break; }
}

docs.title: Functions & Closures
docs.text:
// Function definition
fn add(a, b) {
    a + b                             // Last expr is return value
}

fn greet(name) {
    return "Hello, " + name;          // Explicit return
}

// Closures
let double = |x| x * 2;
let add = |a, b| a + b;

// Closures in array methods
[1, 2, 3].map(|x| x * 2)              // [2, 4, 6]
[1, 2, 3].filter(|x| x > 1)           // [2, 3]

docs.title: Rhai Special Feature: Function-as-Method
docs.text:
Rhai allows calling any function as a method on its first argument:

// These are equivalent:
extract_re(e.line, r"\d+")            // Function call style
e.line.extract_re(r"\d+")             // Method call style

// Use method style for chaining:
e.domain = e.url
    .extract_domain()
    .to_lower()
    .strip();

// Both styles work for all functions:
to_int(e.port)                        // Function style
e.port.to_int()                       // Method style (more readable)

docs.title: Kelora Event Access
docs.text:
The global variable e represents the current event in --filter and --exec stages:

// Direct field access
e.level                               // Top-level field
e.user.name                           // Nested field (maps)
e.scores[1]                           // Array indexing (0-based)
e.scores[-1]                          // Negative indexing (last element)
e.headers["user-agent"]               // Bracket notation for special chars

// Field existence checking
"field" in e                          // Check top-level field exists
e.has_path("user.role")               // Check nested path exists

// Safe field access with defaults
e.get_path("user.role", "guest")      // Get nested with fallback
e.get_path("scores[0]", 0)            // Works with array paths

// Field removal
e.password = ()                       // Remove field (unit assignment)
e.ssn = ()                            // Remove another field
e = ()                                // Remove entire event (filtered out)

docs.title: Array & Map Operations
docs.text:
JSON arrays become native Rhai arrays with full functionality:

// Array transformations
sorted(e.scores)                      // Sort numerically/lexicographically
reversed(e.items)                     // Reverse order
unique(e.tags)                        // Remove duplicates
dedup(e.values)                       // Remove consecutive duplicates
sorted_by(e.users, "age")             // Sort objects by field

// Array methods
e.tags.len()                          // Length
e.tags.is_empty()                     // Check if empty
e.tags.join(", ")                     // Join to string
e.scores.sum()                        // Sum numbers
e.scores.min()                        // Minimum value
e.scores.max()                        // Maximum value

// Array access patterns
if e.items.len() > 0 {
    e.first = e.items[0];
    e.last = e.items[-1];
}

// Fan-out: convert array elements to separate events
emit_each(e.items)                    // Each element becomes an event
emit_each(e.items, #{ctx: "value"})   // Add base fields to each

// Map operations
for (key, val) in e {
    print(`${key} = ${val}`);
}

docs.title: Type Conversions
docs.text:
// Strict conversions (return () on error)
to_int(e.port)                        // String → integer
to_float(e.price)                     // String → float
to_bool(e.active)                     // String → boolean

// Safe conversions with defaults
to_int_or(e.port, 8080)               // Use default if conversion fails
to_float_or(e.price, 0.0)
to_bool_or(e.active, false)

// String conversions
to_string(42)                         // Any → string
e.value.to_int()                      // Method style

// Type checking
type_of(e.field)                      // Get type as string
type_of(e.field) != "()"              // Check if field has value

docs.title: Kelora Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
--begin         // Pre-run once before parsing
                // Populate global `conf` map (becomes read-only)

--filter        // Boolean gate per event
                // true = keep, false = drop
                // Repeatable, executed in order

--exec / -e     // Transform per event
                // Modify event fields
                // Repeatable, executed in order

--exec-file     // Same as --exec, reads script from file

--end           // Post-run once after all processing
                // Access global `metrics` map for reports

Example pipeline:

kelora -f json \
  --begin 'conf.threshold = 100' \
  --filter 'e.count > conf.threshold' \
  --exec 'e.category = if e.count > 1000 { "high" } else { "medium" }' \
  --metrics \
  --exec 'track_sum("total", e.count)' \
  --end 'print("Total: " + metrics.total)'

docs.title: Safe Nested Access
docs.text:
// With default fallback
let role = e.get_path("user.role", "guest");
let port = to_int_or(e.port, 8080);

// With existence check
if e.has_path("user.profile.avatar") {
    e.avatar = e.user.profile.avatar;
}

// Safe array access
if e.items.len() > 0 {
    e.first_item = e.items[0];
}

docs.title: Conditional Field Removal
docs.text:
// Remove debug fields in production
if e.level != "DEBUG" {
    e.stack_trace = ();
    e.debug_info = ();
}

// Remove entire event conditionally
if e.status < 400 { e = (); }         // Only keep errors

docs.title: Method Chaining
docs.text:
// Extract and normalize domain
e.domain = e.url
    .extract_domain()
    .to_lower()
    .strip();

// Parse and extract from structured text
e.error_line = e.stack_trace
    .extract_re(r"line (\d+)", 1)
    .to_int_or(0);

docs.title: Array Processing
docs.text:
// Get top N scores
e.top_3 = sorted(e.scores)[-3:];

// Extract names from sorted users
e.winners = sorted_by(e.users, "score")
    .reverse()
    .map(|u| u.name);

// Filter and count
e.active_items = e.items.filter(|i| i.status == "active");
e.active_count = e.active_items.len();

docs.title: Multi-Level Fan-Out
docs.text:
# First exec: batches → separate events
--exec 'emit_each(e.batches)'

# Second exec: items → separate events with context
--exec 'let ctx = #{batch_id: e.id}; emit_each(e.items, ctx)'

# Filter the final events
--filter 'e.status == "active"'

docs.title: Global Context
docs.text:
conf                                  // Global config map (read-only after --begin)
metrics                               // Global metrics map (from track_* calls)
get_env("VAR", "default")             // Environment variable access

// Example usage:
--begin 'conf.env = get_env("ENVIRONMENT", "dev")'
--filter 'conf.env == "prod" || e.level == "ERROR"'

docs.title: Error Handling Modes
docs.text:
Default (resilient):

  • Parse errors → skip line, continue
  • Filter errors → treat as false, drop event
  • Exec errors → rollback, keep original event

Strict mode (--strict):

  • Any error → abort immediately with exit code 1

docs.title: Rhai Quirks & Gotchas
docs.text:
Coming from Watch out for JavaScript No null/undefined (use ()), no single quotes, let required Python Braces required, no : after if/for, != not <>, double quotes only Rust More permissive syntax, semicolons mostly optional, dynamic typing

Common mistakes:

// ❌ Wrong
x = 1                                 // Error: x not declared
let name = 'alice';                   // Error: single quotes not allowed
if x > 5: print("big")                // Error: colon not allowed, braces required
"5" + 3                               // Error: no implicit conversion

// ✅ Correct
let x = 1;                            // Declare with let
let name = "alice";                   // Double quotes
if x > 5 { print("big"); }            // Braces required
"5".to_int() + 3                      // Explicit conversion

Special behaviors:

  • Last expression in block is return value (no return needed)
  • Semicolons recommended but often optional
  • Function calls without args: e.len same as e.len()
  • No implicit type conversion (use to_int(), to_float(), etc.)

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
// Event manipulation
e.field = value                       // Set field
e.field = ()                          // Remove field
e = ()                                // Remove event

// Type checking
type_of(e.field)                      // Get type
"field" in e                          // Field exists

// Safe access
e.get_path("a.b.c", default)          // Nested with fallback
e.has_path("a.b.c")                   // Check nested exists

// Conversions
to_int_or(val, 0)                     // Safe int conversion
to_float_or(val, 0.0)                 // Safe float conversion
to_bool_or(val, false)                // Safe bool conversion

// Arrays
e.items.len()                         // Length
e.items.is_empty()                    // Check empty
sorted(e.items)                       // Sort
unique(e.items)                       // Deduplicate
emit_each(e.items)                    // Fan out to events

// Strings
e.text.to_lower()                     // Lowercase
e.text.to_upper()                     // Uppercase
e.text.strip()                        // Trim whitespace
e.text.contains("word")               // Substring check
e.text.extract_re(r"(\d+)", 1)        // Regex extraction

// Environment
get_env("VAR", "default")             // Get env var
conf.key                              // Read config (from --begin)
metrics.key                           // Read metrics (in --end)

docs.title: Metrics and Tracking
docs.text: Turn raw log streams into actionable numbers. This tutorial walks through Kelora's metrics pipeline, from basic counters to custom summaries that you can export or feed into dashboards.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Track counts, sums, buckets, and unique values with Rhai helpers
  • Combine --metrics, --stats, --begin, and --end for structured reports
  • Use sliding windows and percentiles for latency analysis
  • Persist metrics to disk for downstream processing

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Completed the Quickstart
  • Familiarity with basic Rhai scripting (--filter, --exec)

docs.title: Sample Data
docs.text:
Commands below use fixtures from the repository. If you cloned the project, the paths resolve relative to the docs root:

  • examples/simple_json.jsonl — mixed application logs
  • examples/window_metrics.jsonl — high-frequency metric samples
  • examples/web_access_large.log.gz — compressed access logs for batch jobs

All commands print real output thanks to markdown-exec; feel free to tweak the expressions and rerun them locally.

docs.title: Step 1 – Quick Counts with track_count()
docs.text:
Count how many events belong to each service while suppressing event output.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

--metrics prints the aggregated map when processing finishes. Use this pattern any time you want a quick histogram after a batch run.

docs.title: Showing Stats at the Same Time
docs.text:
Pair --metrics with --stats when you need throughput details as well:

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

--stats adds processing totals, time span, and field inventory without touching your metrics map.

docs.title: Step 2 – Summaries with Sums, Buckets, and Averages
docs.text:
Kelora ships several helpers for numeric metrics. The following example treats response sizes and latency as rolling aggregates.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found
  • track_sum accumulates totals (suitable for throughput or volume).
  • track_avg automatically maintains a running average per key.
  • track_bucket groups values into ranges so you can build histograms.

Buckets show up as nested maps where each bucket value keeps its own count.

docs.title: Step 3 – Unique Values and Cardinality
docs.text:
track_unique() stores distinct values for a key—handy for unique user counts or cardinality analysis.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

Use metrics["services"].len() later to compute the number of distinct members.

docs.title: Step 4 – Sliding Windows and Percentiles
docs.text:
Enable the window buffer to examine recent events. The example below tracks a five-event moving average and P95 latency for CPU metrics.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

The special window variable becomes available once you pass --window. Use window_numbers(window, FIELD) for numeric arrays and window_values(window, FIELD) for raw strings.

docs.title: Step 5 – Custom Reports with --end
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a formatted report instead of raw maps. Store a short Rhai script and invoke it with --end-file so the same layout works across platforms.

cat <<'RHAI' > metrics_summary.rhai
fn summarize_metrics() {
    let keys = metrics.keys();
    keys.sort();
    for key in keys {
        if !key.starts_with("__op_") {
            print(key + ": " + metrics[key].to_string());
        }
    }
}
RHAI

kelora -f json examples/simple_json.jsonl \
  -F none \
  --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
  --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
  --metrics \
  -I metrics_summary.rhai \
  --end 'summarize_metrics()'

rm metrics_summary.rhai

bash: line 13: kelora: command not found

The automatically printed --metrics block remains, while --end gives you a clean text summary that you can redirect or feed into alerts.

docs.title: Step 6 – Persist Metrics to Disk
docs.text:
Use --metrics-file to serialize the metrics map as JSON for other tools.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found
cat: metrics.json: No such file or directory
rm: cannot remove 'metrics.json': No such file or directory

The JSON structure mirrors the in-memory map, so you can load it with jq, a dashboard agent, or any scripting language.

docs.title: Step 7 – Streaming Scoreboards
docs.text:
Kelora keeps metrics up to date even when tailing files or processing archives. This command watches a gzipped access log and surfaces top status classes.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

Passing --take 0 (or omitting it) keeps processing the entire file. When you run Kelora against a stream (tail -f | kelora ...), the metrics snapshot updates when you terminate the process.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No metrics printed: Ensure you pass --metrics or consume metrics within an --end script. Tracking functions alone do not emit output.
  • Huge maps: Reset counters between runs by clearing your terminal or using rm metrics.json when exporting to disk. Large cardinality sets from track_unique() are the usual culprit.
  • Unexpected __op_* keys: Kelora stores internal operator metadata alongside user metrics. Filter them (as in the metrics_summary.rhai script) before displaying the report.
  • Sliding window functions return empty arrays: window_numbers(window, ...) only works after you enable --window and the requested field exists in the buffered events.

  • Explore the Function Reference for the complete list of tracking helpers and their signatures.

docs.title: Parsing Custom Formats
docs.text: Learn how to parse custom log formats using Kelora's flexible column format specification.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you'll be able to:

  • Parse fixed-width and delimited custom log formats
  • Use column specifications with field names and widths
  • Apply type annotations for automatic conversion
  • Handle timestamp fields and greedy captures
  • Combine custom parsing with filtering and transformation

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Completed the Quickstart
  • Basic understanding of log formats
  • Familiarity with command-line operations

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Many applications generate custom log formats that don't match standard formats like JSON or syslog. Kelora's cols:<spec> format lets you define custom column specifications to parse these logs.

Time: ~15 minutes

docs.title: Step 1: Understanding Column Specifications
docs.text:
The basic syntax for column format is:

-f 'cols:field1:width field2:width field3:*'

Field specification parts: - field1 - Field name - :width - Field width (optional, whitespace-delimited if omitted) - * - Greedy capture (consumes remainder of line)

docs.title: Example Log Format
docs.text:
Let's start with a simple application log:

ERROR api Connection failed
INFO  db  Query executed
WARN  api Slow response time

Each line has three whitespace-delimited fields: level, service, message.

docs.title: Step 2: Basic Whitespace-Delimited Parsing
docs.text:
For whitespace-delimited fields, just list the field names:

bash: line 3: kelora: command not found

How it works: - level - First whitespace-delimited field - service - Second whitespace-delimited field - message - Third whitespace-delimited field (captures rest of line)

docs.title: Step 3: Fixed-Width Fields
docs.text:
For fixed-width columns, specify the character width:

> echo "ERROR     api       Connection failed" | \
    kelora -f 'cols:level:10 service:10 message:*'

Column widths: - level:10 - First 10 characters - service:10 - Next 10 characters - message:* - Remainder of line

The * wildcard must be the last field and consumes everything remaining.

docs.title: Step 4: Adding Type Annotations
docs.text:
Convert fields to specific types using annotations:

> echo "200 1234 0.123
404 5678 0.456
500 9012 0.789" | \
    kelora -f 'cols:status:int bytes:int response_time:float'

Supported types: - :int - Parse as integer - :float - Parse as floating-point number - :bool - Parse as boolean

After type conversion, you can use numeric operations:

> echo "200 1234 0.123" | \
    kelora -f 'cols:status:int bytes:int response_time:float' \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400'

docs.title: Step 5: Handling Timestamps
docs.text:
Use :ts for timestamp fields that Kelora should recognize:

> echo "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z ERROR Connection failed" | \
    kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level message'

The :ts annotation tells Kelora to: - Parse the field as a timestamp - Make it available for time-based filtering (--since, --until) - Use it for time-related functions

docs.title: Step 6: Custom Separators
docs.text:
For non-whitespace separators, use --cols-sep:

> echo "ERROR|api|Connection failed
INFO|db|Query executed" | \
    kelora -f 'cols:level service message' --cols-sep '|'

Works with any separator string:

# Comma-separated
> kelora -f 'cols:level service message' --cols-sep ','

# Tab-separated
> kelora -f 'cols:level service message' --cols-sep $'\t'

# Multi-character separator
> kelora -f 'cols:level service message' --cols-sep ' :: '

docs.title: Step 7: Real-World Example - Application Logs
docs.text:
Let's parse a custom application log format:

Log format: 

[2024-01-15 10:30:00] ERROR api Connection failed to database
[2024-01-15 10:30:01] INFO  db  Query executed successfully
[2024-01-15 10:30:02] WARN  api Slow response: 2500ms

Column specification: 

> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 service:4 message:*' app.log

But the timestamp is wrapped in brackets. We need to extract it first.

docs.title: Using Regex in Exec
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'cols:raw_ts level:5 service:4 message:*' app.log \
    --exec 'e.timestamp = e.raw_ts.extract_re(r"\[(.*?)\]", 1)' \
    --exec 'e.raw_ts = ()' \
    --keys timestamp,level,service,message

What this does: 1. Parse raw_ts as the first field (including brackets) 2. Extract timestamp from brackets using regex 3. Remove raw_ts field (no longer needed) 4. Output cleaned fields

docs.title: Step 8: Combining with Transformations
docs.text:
Parse custom format and add computed fields:

> cat app.log | \
    kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 service:4 message:*' \
    --exec 'if e.message.contains("ms") { e.duration = e.message.extract_re(r"(\d+)ms", 1).to_int() }' \
    --filter 'e.has_path("duration") && e.duration > 1000' \
    --keys timestamp,service,duration,message

Pipeline: 1. Parse custom format 2. Extract duration from message if present 3. Filter for slow requests (>1000ms) 4. Output relevant fields

docs.title: Step 9: Working with Mixed-Width Fields
docs.text:
Some logs have consistent positions but variable content:

ERROR  2024-01-15 Connection failed
INFO   2024-01-15 Query OK
WARN   2024-01-15 High memory usage

Use whitespace delimiter for variable-width fields:

> kelora -f 'cols:level timestamp message' app.log

Or specify exact positions if alignment is strict:

> kelora -f 'cols:level:7 timestamp:11 message:*' app.log

docs.title: Step 10: Complete Example
docs.text:
Let's parse a complex custom format with everything we've learned:

Input log (custom_app.log): 

[2024-01-15 10:30:00] 200 api    1234 0.123 Success
[2024-01-15 10:30:01] 404 web    5678 0.456 Not found
[2024-01-15 10:30:02] 500 api    9012 0.789 Server error

Parse specification: 

> kelora -f 'cols:raw_ts status:int service:7 bytes:int latency:float message:*' custom_app.log \
    --exec 'e.timestamp = e.raw_ts.extract_re(r"\[(.*?)\]", 1)' \
    --exec 'e.raw_ts = ()' \
    --exec 'e.is_error = e.status >= 400' \
    --exec 'e.is_slow = e.latency > 0.5' \
    --filter 'e.is_error || e.is_slow' \
    --keys timestamp,status,service,message

What happens: 1. Parse fields with type annotations 2. Extract timestamp from brackets 3. Add is_error flag for HTTP errors 4. Add is_slow flag for high latency 5. Filter for errors or slow requests 6. Output cleaned fields

docs.title: Pattern 1: Log Level + Message
docs.text: > kelora -f 'cols:level message' app.log --levels error,warn

docs.title: Pattern 2: Timestamp + Level + Service + Message
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level:5 service:10 message:*' app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"'

docs.title: Pattern 3: Fixed-Width with Type Conversion
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'cols:status:int bytes:int duration:float path:*' access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
    --exec 'track_avg("latency", e.duration)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Pattern 4: Extract and Transform
docs.text:
> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp level data:*' app.log \
    --exec 'e.values = e.data.split(",")' \
    --exec 'e.count = e.values.len()' \
    --keys timestamp,level,count

docs.title: Use Whitespace Delimiters When Possible
docs.text:
Simpler and more flexible:

# Good - whitespace delimited
> kelora -f 'cols:level service message' app.log

# Avoid unless necessary - fixed width
> kelora -f 'cols:level:10 service:10 message:*' app.log

docs.title: Use Type Annotations Early
docs.text:
Convert types during parsing, not in exec:

# Good - parse as int
> kelora -f 'cols:status:int bytes:int' --filter 'e.status >= 400'

# Less efficient - convert in exec
> kelora -f 'cols:status bytes' --exec 'e.status = e.status.to_int()' --filter 'e.status >= 400'

docs.title: Name Fields Descriptively
docs.text:
# Good
> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp level service message'

# Less clear
> kelora -f 'cols:col1 col2 col3 col4'

docs.title: Use Greedy Capture for Messages
docs.text:
Always use * for the last field if it's a message:

> kelora -f 'cols:level service message:*'

docs.title: Combine with Extract Prefix
docs.text:
For Docker Compose-style logs:

> docker compose logs | \
    kelora --extract-prefix container \
           -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level message:*'

docs.title: Fields Not Parsing Correctly
docs.text:
Problem: Fields are misaligned or missing.

Solution: Check separator and field widths: 

# Debug by outputting all fields
> kelora -f 'cols:field1 field2 field3:*' app.log --take 3

# Try different separator
> kelora -f 'cols:field1 field2 field3' --cols-sep '|' app.log --take 3

docs.title: Timestamp Not Recognized
docs.text:
Problem: Timestamp field not working with --since.

Solution: Use :ts annotation and verify format: 

> kelora -f 'cols:timestamp:ts level message' app.log --ts-format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'

docs.title: Type Conversion Failures
docs.text:
Problem: Integer/float conversions failing.

Solution: Use get_path with defaults in resilient mode: 

> kelora -f 'cols:status bytes' --exec 'e.status_int = to_int_or(e.status, 0)'

docs.title: Greedy Field Capturing Too Much
docs.text:
Problem: Last field includes separators.

Solution: Be specific with earlier fields: 

# If fields are fixed width, specify widths
> kelora -f 'cols:level:10 service:10 message:*'

docs.text:
Now that you understand custom format parsing, explore:

  • Working with Time - Advanced timestamp handling
  • Format Reference - Complete format documentation
  • Scripting Transforms - Advanced event transformation

docs.text:

docs.title: Scripting Transforms
docs.text: Master Kelora's Rhai scripting stages to reshape events, enrich payloads, and fan out nested structures. This guide focuses on practical patterns you can drop into your own pipelines.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• Normalize inconsistent fields and add derived values
  • Build multi-stage transformations with --exec
  • Validate and discard malformed events safely
  • Fan out nested arrays and preserve context
  • Share reusable helpers with --include / --exec-file
  • Understand resilient vs strict error handling

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Completed the Quickstart
  • Reviewed Metrics and Tracking for pipeline context

docs.title: Step 1 – Normalize Fields Safely
docs.text:
Start with examples/errors_exec_transform.jsonl, which includes messy values.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

to_int_or(value, fallback) converts strings to integers and substitutes the fallback when conversion fails. Stacking --exec scripts lets you layer transformations without writing monolithic expressions.

docs.title: Step 2 – Derive New Fields and Filter by Them
docs.text:
Use the normalized values to add severity classification, then keep only error events.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

Filters run between exec scripts. Any fields you create earlier are immediately available to later filters or transformations.

docs.title: Step 3 – Guard Against Bad Data
docs.text:
Kelora defaults to resilient mode: exec errors roll back the event and processing continues. Still, it is better to guard the data and drop malformed records explicitly.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

e = () removes the event from the pipeline. The type check avoids runtime errors when the tags field contains a string instead of an array.

Warning

Add --strict if you want Kelora to abort on the first error instead of skipping bad events. Strict mode is ideal for CI pipelines where silent fallback would hide problems.

docs.title: Step 4 – Fan Out Nested Data
docs.text:
emit_each() converts arrays into individual events while keeping context. The orders fixture demonstrates nested arrays that you can flatten in two stages.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

The first exec fans out orders while copying batch metadata. The second exec fans out individual items, enriching each emitted event with both batch and order identifiers.

docs.title: Step 5 – Window-Aware Enrichment
docs.text:
Enable the sliding window to compare the current event to recent history.

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

window holds the current event plus the previous N events (here N = 3). Using window_numbers(window, FIELD) avoids manual parsing and gracefully skips missing values.

docs.title: Step 6 – Reuse Logic with --include and --exec-file
docs.text:
Keep complex logic in separate files. The snippet below defines a helper and reuses it across multiple commands.

cat <<'RHAI' > classifiers.rhai
fn classify_status(status) {
    let code = to_int_or(status, -1);
    if code >= 500 {
        "critical"
    } else if code >= 400 {
        "error"
    } else if code >= 200 {
        "ok"
    } else {
        "other"
    }
}
RHAI

kelora -f json examples/errors_exec_transform.jsonl \
  -I classifiers.rhai \
  --exec 'e.severity = classify_status(e.status)' \
  --keys timestamp,status,severity \
  -F json --take 3
rm classifiers.rhai

bash: line 16: kelora: command not found

You can also move long exec blocks to a dedicated Rhai file:

kelora -f json app.jsonl --exec-file transforms.rhai

Put shared helpers under scripts/ or dev/ and version them alongside your pipeline definitions.

docs.title: Step 7 – Understand Error Handling Semantics
docs.text:
• Resilient mode (default): Kelora rolls back the event when an exec throws and prints a warning. The pipeline continues with the next event. Use this for exploratory work and long-running tail sessions.
  • Strict mode (--strict): The first exec error stops the process with exit code 1. Ideal for CI, production batch jobs, or when you have unit tests guarding your scripts.
  • Filtering events: Set e = () to drop a record after you detect invalid data. This is preferable to letting bad events fail later stages.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
• Function not found: Ensure supporting files are loaded via -I or --exec-file, and double-check spelling—Rhai treats names as case-sensitive.
  • Unexpected fields missing: Remember that filters remove events between exec stages. If a later exec cannot find a field, verify the event survived the earlier filters.
  • Decimal precision: Functions like round(value) operate on whole numbers. Multiply before rounding (round(value * 100.0) / 100.0) to keep two decimal places.
  • Fan-out explosion: Each emit_each can multiply events. Add guard conditions (if e.has_path("orders")) to avoid emitting empty rows.

docs.text:
